passage: The flat in Lisbon had no internet yet, so Paulo sat at the kitchen table with Soo-ah's laptop, comparing broadband plans. Basic: 100 Mbps, €25. Plus: 300 Mbps, €44, two-year contract. Ultra: 1 Gbps, €45, same contract, free router. "Soo-ah, Ultra is basically free!" he said, finger already on the button. Then he stopped. Who would ever pay €44 for Plus when Ultra was one euro more? Nobody. Plus was there to make Ultra shine. He covered the Plus row with a sticky note and looked again. Basic against Ultra: twenty euros a month apart. "What do we actually do online?" he asked. Soo-ah shrugged. "Stream shows. Video calls with my mum." Paulo peeled off the note and clicked Basic.

qa.q: How much was the Plus plan?
qa.a: €44, with a two-year contract.

qa.q: What did Paulo realise when he stopped before clicking?
qa.a: He felt suspicious once he saw nobody would pay €44 for Plus when Ultra was one euro more, so Plus seemed to exist only to make Ultra look like a bargain. 🤔

qa.q: What did Paulo do after spotting the odd plan, and why did it help?
qa.a: He covered the Plus row and asked what they actually do online; comparing only Basic and Ultra against real needs showed Basic was enough.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah feel about the choice, given how they use the internet?
qa.a: Soo-ah only needs shows and video calls, so Basic probably feels fine, and Soo-ah may be glad not to be locked into paying for speed they won't use.

grounding: A young man comparing broadband plans notices an oddly poor option making another look excellent, then asks what they really need without it.

passage: In the HR room at the textile office, Hafsa spread three insurance add-on brochures in front of Nitin. "Every new joiner picks one by Friday." Silver: basic cover, a small monthly cut. Gold: slightly more cover, with a cut nearly as big as Platinum's. Platinum: much more cover, for just a little more than Gold. Nitin's pen hovered over Platinum. Gold looked silly next to it, and Platinum looked brilliant. He frowned. "Hafsa, does anyone ever choose Gold?" She laughed. "Almost never." Nitin sat back. If Gold weren't there, would Platinum still look brilliant? He wrote down what he actually needed: cover for his parents, who lived with him. Then he asked for a day to read each brochure properly at home.

qa.q: How many brochures did Hafsa spread in front of Nitin?
qa.a: Three insurance add-on brochures.

qa.q: Why did Nitin frown with his pen over Platinum?
qa.a: He noticed Gold looked silly and Platinum brilliant, and suspected the odd middle option was shaping his feeling rather than his own needs.

qa.q: What steps did Nitin take after spotting the pattern?
qa.a: He asked whether anyone chose Gold, wrote down what he actually needed, cover for his parents, and took a day to read the brochures at home before choosing.

qa.a: Hafsa laughs because she knows almost nobody picks Gold; she may be amused, but the question also shows how the layout nudges new joiners without them noticing.

passage:
Hi Urmila,
Quick update on the phone plan for Maa, since you asked me to sort it. The shop showed three: ₹199 with 1 GB a day, ₹449 with 1.5 GB a day, and ₹479 with 3 GB a day plus a video app. The man kept saying, "For thirty rupees more, you get double!" and honestly, I nearly signed. Then I noticed the ₹449 one was strange. Why would anyone pick it? It only seemed to exist to make ₹479 look like a gift. So I asked myself what Maa actually does on her phone: video calls with us, bhajans in the morning, a few forwards. She has never used 1 GB in a day. So I've taken the ₹199 one. If she needs more, we can change it next month.
Sumit

qa.q: What does Maa use her phone for?
qa.a: Video calls, bhajans in the morning and a few forwards.

qa.q: What made Sumit nearly sign for the ₹479 plan?
qa.a: The shopkeeper kept saying "double for thirty rupees more", and next to ₹449 the bigger plan felt like a gift, so Sumit was drawn to it.

qa.q: Which question helped Sumit decide, and why?
qa.a: Asking what Maa actually does on her phone; measured against her real use, ₹199 was enough, whatever the ₹449 plan made the others look like.

qa.q: How might Maa be affected by Sumit's choice?
qa.a: Maa gets a plan that fits how she uses the phone and can still get more if needed, without anyone paying for data and apps she won't touch. 🙂

grounding: A young adult choosing a phone plan notices an oddly poor option makes the priciest look excellent, then decides by what Maa needs.

passage: Shalini, you'll like this. So, I'm Lalremsiami, the one who never reads fine print, and I finally bought the laptop for work. At the counter in Aizawl, the salesman slid over a card for damage cover. One year, basic: twelve hundred. Two years, no accidental damage: twenty-nine hundred. Two years, full cover with accidental damage: twenty-nine ninety-nine. He tapped the last one. 'Madam, ninety-nine rupees more for full protection.' And honestly? My hand was already on my wallet. It looked so obviously smart. Then I thought, wait. Who on earth buys the middle one? Nobody. It's there so the last one looks like a gift. So I stood there and asked myself what I'd choose if the middle one didn't exist. The laptop sits on my desk at home. It never leaves the room. I took the basic cover. He looked a bit disappointed. I felt like I'd solved a puzzle.

qa.q: How much was the full two-year cover with accidental damage?
qa.a: It was twenty-nine ninety-nine.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel right before noticing the middle option was odd?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt confident and eager to pay, because the full cover looked obviously smart, like a gift next to the middle one.

qa.q: Which question helped Lalremsiami decide, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Asking what to choose if the middle option didn't exist, and remembering the laptop never leaves the room, led to the basic cover.

qa.q: How might the salesman see Lalremsiami's choice?
qa.a: The salesman looked a bit disappointed, likely because the layout of the card usually steers buyers to the pricier cover.

grounding: A young adult buying laptop cover notices an oddly poor middle option making the top plan look excellent, then pauses to ask what is actually needed.

passage: I'm Himani, and I share a flat in Pune with Pallavi. Last Sunday she was choosing our internet plan on her laptop while I made tea. I heard her read them out. 'Plan A, 40 Mbps, six hundred a month. Plan B, 100 Mbps, twelve hundred, but only on a two-year lock-in. Plan C, 150 Mbps, twelve-fifty, no lock-in, free router.' She said, 'C, obviously. B is terrible.' Then she went quiet for a long time. I don't know exactly what she was thinking. But she opened a notebook and wrote two lines: 'Two people. Video calls, one movie a week.' Then she covered B with her hand and said, 'If this one wasn't here, would C still look amazing?' She looked at A for a while. In the end she chose A and set a reminder to check the speed after a month. I would have clicked C in two seconds.

qa.q: What did Pallavi write in her notebook?
qa.a: She wrote two lines: 'Two people. Video calls, one movie a week.'

qa.q: What does Pallavi's long quiet suggest about her after saying 'C, obviously'?
qa.a: It suggests she started to doubt her first reaction and wondered whether plan B was making C look better than it was.

qa.q: What did Pallavi do before choosing, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She covered plan B and compared the rest against their real needs, so the poor option stopped steering her toward the pricier plan.

qa.q: How might Himani's own habits change after watching Pallavi?
qa.a: Himani admits to clicking C in two seconds usually, so Himani might start pausing to check real needs too.

grounding: A flatmate watches a young woman notice that a poor broadband option made another look excellent, then pause and choose by their actual needs.
